newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian business confidence rises - survey.
newsitem.headline: Australian business confidence rises - survey.

text.p: Australian business confidence rose slightly in the June quarter in response to the May 13 national budget and the latest interest rate cut 10 days later, a survey released on Tuesday showed.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) and Westpac Banking Corp survey of industrial trends also found that the employment market improved in the June quarter, but was expected to weaken in the next three months.
ACCI chief executive Mark Paterson said he believed the interest rate cut on May 23 was largely responsible for the rise in confidence, although the budget had also sent positive signals to business.
Manufacturers predicting an improvement in the general business situation in the next six months climbed to 42 percent from 35 percent in the March quarter.
"I think that it's a combination of the two factors, but there's no doubt that the reduction in interest rates has had a positive impact," Paterson told reporters.
But he said there was unlikely to be a substantial improvement in the labour market until economic growth lifted to between four and 4.5 percent.
"We will only make serious inroads in relation to employment when we get the rate of growth up," Paterson said.
"It will depend critically how quickly we can get that rate of growth up and how long we can sustain it."
Figures released last week showed Australia's seasonally adjusted average gross domestic product rose 0.9 percent in the March quarter. Real GDP-A in the year to March rose 2.4 percent.
Australian unemployment was 8.7 percent in April and has been stuck at or above 8.5 percent for the past year.
"I think that we've got reasonable expectations that we will get the unemployment level below eight percent, but putting a time frame on that is really just an exercise in guessing," Paterson said.
The survey found expectations for an upturn in orders and production were continuing to fall short, but higher outcomes were again forecast for the September quarter.
Capacity utilisation remained low but was rising, while export deliveries increased in the June quarter with further strong rises predicted for the September quarter.

"This is a significant reversal from the weak performance in the March quarter and reflects improving conditions in export markets and the early benefits of a lower, more competitive currency," Paterson said.
Inflationary pressures remained well under control with average selling prices falling for the seventh consecutive quarter and costs remaining steady.
The survey found costs were expected to drop over the next three months.
